slides.headline: The problem version control solves
slides.body: In one sentence: a version control system records successive states of a set of files, so that you can recall any state, compare any two, and see who recorded each one, when, and why.

slides.headline: Git's design goals
slides.body: Git was written in 2005 for the Linux kernel, after the kernel project lost free use of the proprietary tool BitKeeper.

slides.direction: The goals table of section 1.4.

rows: Almost every operation reads local files
Four object types named by a hash of their content, plus names that point at them
Strong support for non-linear development (thousands of parallel branches)
A branch is one small name that points at a commit, so creating one costs almost nothing
Every clone has the history; fetch and push exchange objects and update names
Able to handle large projects like the Linux kernel efficiently
Compressed pack files; later, partial clone and sparse checkout

slides.body: And one note on the other layer.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Saying "it is committed" to mean "it is on the server". Root cause: commit and publish are different operations; git commit writes to your disk and git push copies commits to another repository.
Treating origin/main as the live state of the server. Root cause: it is a cached copy, the last-known state as of your last exchange.

Assuming a clone is a backup that somebody made for you. Root cause: distributed means that copies are possible, not that they are made; a commit that exists only on one laptop is one disk failure away from not existing.
Looking for a pull request, a review or a ruleset inside Git. Root cause: those are GitHub objects in GitHub's database, and they do not arrive with a clone.
A command from the course is "not a git command". Root cause: the shell found the Apple Git first; which -a git and git --version show it, and the fix is to put the Homebrew directory first in PATH.

beats.text: Someone on your team writes one short line in chat: "The merge is blocked." A merge combines two lines of work into one. Your CTO asks why.
beats.tele: Someone on your team writes one short line in chat: "The merge is blocked." A merge combines two lines of work into one. Your CTO asks why.

beats.text: That one sentence has three different root causes, in three different layers. Git stops a merge when both sides changed the same lines. GitHub stops a merge when a ruleset, a named list of rules the platform enforces, requires a review that hasn't been given. And GitHub Actions, the part of GitHub that runs automated jobs, stops a merge when a required check hasn't reported success. The three symptoms look alike in a chat message, and the three fixes have nothing in common.

beats.text: Centralized versus distributed. In one sentence: in a centralized system the history lives on one server and each developer holds one checked-out version. In a distributed system every developer's copy contains the history, and "the server" is one more copy that the team agrees to treat as the meeting point. Such a copy is called a clone.
beats.tele: Centralized versus distributed. In one sentence: in a centralized system the history lives on one server and each developer holds one checked-out version. In a distributed system every developer's copy contains the history, and "the server" is one more copy that the team agrees to treat as the meeting point. Such a copy is called a clone.

beats.text: Compare the two by four questions. Where does the history live? Centralized: on one server. Distributed: in every clone. How is a change recorded? Centralized: a network operation against the server. Distributed: a local write, and publishing is a separate step. What if the server is unreachable? Centralized: nobody can record changes or collaborate. Distributed: local work continues, and the exchange waits. What if the server's disk is lost and there are no backups? Centralized: the history is gone. Distributed: every clone still holds what it had fetched.

beats.text: Three consequences shape your daily work with Git. One: commit and publish are different operations. A commit is one saved snapshot of your whole project, with a note about who saved it and why. git commit writes to the repository on your disk. git push copies commits to another repository. "It is committed" and "it is on the server" are independent facts, checked with different commands.

beats.text: So where does a repository live? The whole repository, meaning the history and every name in it, is the dot git directory at the top of your project. A clone is a copy of another repository's objects and names. And the copy on a server is normally a bare repository: the same contents, with no checked-out files beside them.

beats.text: Git's manual describes it as "a fast, scalable, distributed revision control system with an unusually rich command set that provides both high-level operations and full access to internals". The high-level commands, such as git add, git commit and git merge, are called porcelain. The low-level ones, such as git hash-object and git update-ref, are called plumbing. This course uses plumbing to prove what porcelain did.

GitHub is a hosted service that stores Git repositories and surrounds them with its own objects: accounts, permissions, pull requests, reviews, rulesets and workflows.

GitHub is a hosted service that stores Git repositories and surrounds them with its own objects: accounts, permissions, pull requests, reviews, rulesets and workflows.

beats.text: Try it now, on paper. Draw two columns, Git and GitHub. Place three things: a branch, a pull request, and the "Verified" badge next to a commit. Thirty seconds. Keep the paper, and check your answers as we fill the real table.

beats.text: Fill the two columns with me, and for each row ask: does it arrive with git clone? Commits, directory trees, file contents and annotated tags: Git, objects in the repository, and yes, they arrive. Branches and tags: Git, names in the repository, and yes. The server's branches arrive as remote-tracking branches such as origin/main. So your branch belongs in the Git column.

The server's branches arrive as remote-tracking branches such as `origin/main`. So your branch belongs in the Git column.

beats.text: Author and committer name and email, and a signature: Git, inside each commit. But the "Verified" badge next to a commit: GitHub. It's GitHub's judgement of the signature, stored in GitHub's database, and it doesn't arrive with a clone. If you put it under Git, that's the usual first answer.

beats.text: HEAD, the index, reflogs, stashes, hooks and the config file in the dot git folder: Git, but local only. Each clone has its own. You'll meet every one of them in Part 1.

beats.text: A pull request, a review, a comment: GitHub's database, plus read-only refs, which are names, that GitHub creates on the server for the pull request's commits. Issues, discussions, stars: GitHub. A fork: GitHub, a server-side repository linked to its parent. To Git it's one more remote. Rulesets and branch protection: GitHub settings. A release: a GitHub object that points at a Git tag and adds notes and files, so the tag arrives and the release doesn't.

A release: a GitHub object that points at a Git tag and adds notes and files, so the tag arrives and the release doesn't.

beats.text: A workflow file, in the workflows folder under dot github: Git, because it's a tracked file in commits. A workflow run, its logs, its artifacts and its secrets: GitHub Actions. Access tokens, SSH keys and collaborator roles: GitHub.

beats.text: One row deserves its own sentence. A pull request is not a Git feature. Git has commits, branches and merges.
beats.tele: One row deserves its own sentence. A pull request is not a Git feature. Git has commits, branches and merges.

beats.text: GitHub adds the pull request as a place to discuss a proposed merge.
beats.tele: GitHub adds the pull request as a place to discuss a proposed merge.

beats.text: And GitHub performs the merge on its servers when you press the button.
beats.tele: And GitHub performs the merge on its servers when you press the button.

beats.text: Three pictures now. The textbook gives one analogy for each idea, and each has a breaking point that teaches more than the analogy.
beats.tele: Three pictures now. The textbook gives one analogy for each idea, and each has a breaking point that teaches more than the analogy.

beats.text: For version control: a bound laboratory notebook. Pages are numbered, dated and signed, and a correction is a new page, never an erased one. It breaks in two places. A notebook is one sequence kept by one person, while a repository holds many lines of work that people extend in parallel and later join. And each recorded state in Git is the whole project, not that day's notes.
beats.tele: For version control: a bound laboratory notebook. Pages are numbered, dated and signed, and a correction is a new page, never an erased one. It breaks in two places. A notebook is one sequence kept by one person, while a repository holds many lines of work that people extend in parallel and later join. And each recorded state in Git is the whole project, not that day's notes.

beats.text: For centralized versus distributed: a centralized system is a reference library. The books stay in the building, and when the building is closed nobody reads. A distributed system gives every reader a copy of the whole library.
beats.tele: For centralized versus distributed: a centralized system is a reference library. The books stay in the building, and when the building is closed nobody reads. A distributed system gives every reader a copy of the whole library.

beats.text: It breaks because library copies never need to agree again, while repositories must. Each copy accumulates its own additions. Exchanging them is an explicit act, a fetch or a push, and it can find two copies in disagreement.
beats.tele: It breaks because library copies never need to agree again, while repositories must. Each copy accumulates its own additions. Exchanging them is an explicit act, a fetch or a push, and it can find two copies in disagreement.

beats.text: For Git and GitHub: Git is a file format with its editor, and GitHub is a document-management service where such files are stored, discussed and approved. It breaks because GitHub also runs Git on its servers and performs Git operations for you: pressing a merge button creates commits. Platform actions change Git data, so you must know which layer did what.

It breaks because GitHub also runs Git on its servers and performs Git operations for you: pressing a merge button creates commits. Platform actions change Git data, so you must know which layer did what.

beats.text: On the left, one server holds the only history. Asha and Ravi each hold one version, and every commit is an arrow to the server: a network operation. On the right, the server is a bare repository with the history, and Asha and Ravi each hold the history plus one checked-out version. The arrows are now push and fetch. Commit doesn't appear as an arrow at all, because a commit is local. That missing arrow is the difference.

beats.text: Enough theory. Before we trust any transcript, we find out which Git produced it. This script is marked volatile, because its output is specific to the machine: the verification tool checks that it runs and doesn't compare its output. Your paths may differ from mine.

beats.text: The first command is which -a git, which lists every match in search order. Predict: how many lines will it print on your Mac? Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: The first line is the program that runs when you type git. On this machine it's the Homebrew build, and it prints version 2.55.0. Homebrew is a tool that installs software on a Mac. /usr/bin/git is the Git that Apple ships with its developer tools, and it prints 2.50.1. The third line repeats the first, because the Homebrew directory appears twice in this shell's PATH, the list of folders the shell searches. That's harmless.
beats.tele: The first line is the program that runs when you type `git`. On this machine it's the Homebrew build, and it prints version 2.55.0. Homebrew is a tool that installs software on a Mac. `/usr/bin/git` is the Git that Apple ships with its developer tools, and it prints 2.50.1. The third line repeats the first, because the Homebrew directory appears twice in this shell's `PATH`, the list of folders the shell searches. That's harmless.

beats.text: The difference matters. Git 2.50.1 has no git history and no git last-modified, and its manual still labels git switch and git restore as experimental, a label that Git removed in 2.51. Each installation also reads its own system-level configuration file. You meet the Apple Git in three situations. A script that calls /usr/bin/git by its full path. A scheduled job or graphical tool that starts with a shorter PATH than your terminal. And a colleague's Mac without Homebrew.

A scheduled job or graphical tool that starts with a shorter `PATH` than your terminal. And a colleague's Mac without Homebrew.

beats.text: Now ask the Git that answered how it was built.

beats.text: Three lines are worth reading now. default-hash: sha1 means new repositories name objects with SHA-1. SHA-1: SHA1_DC means the implementation detects known collision attacks. And default-ref-format: files means branch and tag names are stored as plain files, which is why this course can show them with cat. Chapter 3 covers the alternatives.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Saying "it is committed" to mean "it is on the server". Root cause: commit and publish are different operations; git commit writes to your disk and git push copies commits to another repository.
beats.tele: Saying "it is committed" to mean "it is on the server". Root cause: commit and publish are different operations; `git commit` writes to your disk and `git push` copies commits to another repository.

beats.text: Treating origin/main as the live state of the server. Root cause: it is a cached copy, the last-known state as of your last exchange.
beats.tele: Treating `origin/main` as the live state of the server. Root cause: it is a cached copy, the last-known state as of your last exchange.

beats.text: Assuming a clone is a backup that somebody made for you. Root cause: distributed means that copies are possible, not that they are made; a commit that exists only on one laptop is one disk failure away from not existing.
beats.tele: Assuming a clone is a backup that somebody made for you. Root cause: distributed means that copies are possible, not that they are made; a commit that exists only on one laptop is one disk failure away from not existing.

beats.text: Looking for a pull request, a review or a ruleset inside Git. Root cause: those are GitHub objects in GitHub's database, and they do not arrive with a clone.

beats.text: A command from the course is "not a git command". Root cause: the shell found the Apple Git first; which -a git and git --version show it, and the fix is to put the Homebrew directory first in PATH.

Datasets and model weights need additional tools, which later chapters cover.
